newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian unions call for condemnation of S.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Australian unions call for condemnation of S.Korea.

text.p: Australia's top union body, the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU), called on Friday for the Australian government to condemn South Korea's new labour law, which has sparked major industrial unrest in that country.

The ACTU asked for Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer to demand at the next meeting of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) that the South Korean government withdraw the legislation.
The ruling New Korea Party pushed through the labour law on December 26 during a secret dawn session of parliament when opposition political parties were absent.
More than three weeks of sporadic work stoppages in South Korea were sparked by the passage of the law, which gives employers the right to lay off workers, replace strikers and extend work hours.
The ACTU also wants Downer to ask the South Korean government to halt the arrests of union officials and to begin negotiations with the trade unions for genuine reform to labour legislation.
Four South Korean union heads have already been seized and arrest warrants are in force for 16 others.

"On two occasions in 1996, the Australian government accepted the assurances of the Korean government that it would reform the Korean labour laws in conformity with international labour standards," ACTU president Jennie George said.
She said instead, Australia resigned its candidacy for the International Labour Organisation governing body to allow Korea to take a position.
Australia then supported Korea's membership of the OECD on the basis of its assurances that it would reform industrial relations laws in line with international standards, she said.
A spokesman for Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs said Downer had received a letter from the ACTU in which it outlined its concerns.
"We are looking at a response to that letter at the moment," the spokesman told Reuters.

International labour organisations have stepped up their pressure on South Korea to dump the law. Ten leaders of trade union organisations are due in Seoul next week to replace four others who left on Thursday.
